cells.title: Overview
cells.source: This notebook ports DEFINE-SIMPLE 1.1 (Dafermos and Nikolaidi 2026). Firms, households and banks interact in a growing global economy whose carbon intensity falls when green capital rises relative to conventional capital. Period 1 is calendar year 2023; the baseline runs through 2100.
cells.more:
**DEFINE-SIMPLE** is the teaching core of the DEFINE (Dynamic Ecosystem-FINance-Economy)
framework. It keeps three sectors — households, firms and banks — and one ecological
channel: fossil CO2 emissions track output through a carbon intensity that depends on
the green-to-conventional capital ratio.

The executable equations and 2023 calibration come from the Model Builder export in
`references/define-simple-1.1/DEFINE_SIMPLE.R` (DEFINE-model/SIMPLE-1.1). That script
accompanies Dafermos Y. and Nikolaidi M. (2026), _Ecological stock-flow consistent
modelling: a theoretical and practical guide_, in D'Alessandro, Distefano and Morlin
(eds.), _Handbook of Ecological Macroeconomics_. The full DEFINE-GLOBAL model adds
climate damages, QE and material balances; this notebook stays with SIMPLE 1.1.

Demand is almost recursive inside each year. Consumption and investment use lagged
income, deposits, the profit rate and the capital stock, then `Y = CO + I`. Banks
create deposits when they make loans, and the redundant check is `D = D_red` with
`D_red = L`. Capital does not depreciate: `K_G = lag(K_G) + I_G`.

The baseline is a balanced-growth path at `g_Y = 0.029`. Because the initial
`K_G / K_C` already equals `beta / (1 - beta)`, that ratio (and therefore `CI`) stays
flat until a scenario changes the green investment share.

cells.title: DEFINE-SIMPLE balance sheet
cells.description: Balance-sheet matrix for households, firms and banks.
cells.note: Validated against the DEFINE-SIMPLE 1.1 R baseline (D = L).
cells.more:
Households hold only deposits `D`. Firms own conventional and green capital
(`K_C`, `K_G`) and owe conventional and green loans (`L_C`, `L_G`). Banks hold
those loans as assets and issue deposits, so bank net worth is `L - D`. The hidden
equation keeps `D = L`, and therefore bank net worth at zero.

Firm net worth is the real capital stock not financed by loans, `K - L`. Household
wealth equals the deposit stock. Reading assets as positive and liabilities as
negative, every financial row sums across sectors to zero; the capital rows are
the non-financial assets that net worth has to match.

cells.title: DEFINE-SIMPLE transactions-flow matrix
cells.description: Transactions-flow matrix with a split current/capital account for firms.
cells.more:
Household disposable income is wages plus distributed firm profits plus bank
profits plus deposit interest. What is not consumed is added to deposits, so the
household column is the identity `D = lag(D) + Y_H - CO`.

Firms sell consumption and both green and conventional investment goods, pay
wages and green/conventional loan interest, and split profits into dividends
`DP` and retained earnings `RP`. Retained earnings plus new green and
conventional loans finance capital accumulation:
`d(L_G) = I_G - beta * RP` and `d(L_C) = I_C - (1 - beta) * RP`. Banks earn
the spread between loan and deposit rates and distribute all profits `BP` to
households, so they hold no own funds.

cells.title: DEFINE-SIMPLE transaction flow sequence
cells.description: Sequence view generated from the transactions-flow matrix at the selected simulation period.

cells.title: Green capital and carbon intensity
cells.source: Carbon intensity `CI` is a decreasing function of the lagged green-to-conventional capital ratio. Emissions are `EMIS_F = CI * Y`. In the baseline that ratio is constant, so intensity is flat and emissions grow with output.
cells.more:
Green investment is a share `beta` of total investment. That share responds to the
loan-rate differential, `beta = beta_0 - beta_1 * (int_G - int_C)`. A higher
`K_G / K_C` then lowers carbon intensity through a logistic (Hill) curve between
`CI_min` and `CI_max`:

`CI = CI_min + (CI_max - CI_min) / (1 + pow((lag(K_G) / lag(K_C)) / c_CI, k_CI))`

The 2023 calibration sets `K_G / K_C = beta / (1 - beta)`, so both capital stocks
grow at the same rate on the baseline and `CI` never moves. The green-investment
scenario raises `beta` and that is what pulls intensity down.

cells.title: DEFINE-SIMPLE 1.1 model

equations.name: TP
equations.expression: Y - W - int_C * lag(L_C) - int_G * lag(L_G)

equations.name: BP
equations.expression: int_C * lag(L_C) + int_G * lag(L_G) - int_D * lag(D)

equations.name: CI
equations.expression: CI_min + (CI_max - CI_min) / (1 + pow((lag(K_G) / lag(K_C)) / c_CI, k_CI))

cells.more:
Consumption and investment are predetermined from lags, so Gauss–Seidel has little
simultaneous work once `Y = CO + I` is known. Green and conventional loans split
the financing of investment after retained profits: a share `beta` of retained
earnings is attributed to green projects.

`D` is the household wealth accumulation identity and is redundant given the bank
balance-sheet residual `D_red = L`. The solver checks `D = D_red` rather than
dropping one of the two equations.

cells.title: Externals

externals.name: c_1
externals.desc: Propensity to consume out of disposable income.

externals.name: c_2
externals.desc: Propensity to consume out of deposits.

externals.name: alpha_1
externals.desc: Sensitivity of investment to the profit rate.

externals.name: beta_1
externals.desc: Sensitivity of green investment share to the loan-rate gap.

externals.name: c_CI
externals.desc: Green-to-conventional ratio at which CI is midway.

cells.more:
These values are the 2023 calibration after the R Model Builder has iterated
`Parameters_InitialValues` to a fixed point. They are frozen numbers, not the
circular init formulae. `c_1`, `s_F`, `alpha_0`, `v`, `c_CI` and `k_CI` are
implied by World Bank / BIS / Global Carbon Budget stocks for 2023 and the
assumed balanced-growth rate of 2.9 percent.

cells.title: Initial values
cells.more:
Period 1 (displayed as the first sample point) is the 2023 data-consistent
snapshot from R, not a Gauss–Seidel solve of the behavioural equations. From
period 2 the notebook uses the same identities as `Equations()` in
`DEFINE_SIMPLE.R`. Putting the 2023 stocks here means lags in period 2 are the
calibrated 2023 values.

cells.title: Baseline run
cells.description: DEFINE-SIMPLE 1.1 baseline, 2023–2100, with hidden condition D = D_red.

cells.title: Baseline output, growth and leverage
cells.more:
The baseline is balanced growth. Output `Y` starts at `106.94` in 2023 and reaches
about `966` by 2100, compounding at `g_Y = 0.029`. Utilisation `u` stays at `0.73`,
leverage `lev` at about `0.101`, and the profit rate `r` at about `0.040`. Those
ratios are pinned by the 2023 calibration; nothing in the baseline disturbs them.

cells.title: Baseline green share, intensity and emissions
cells.more:
`beta` is constant because `int_G = int_C`. Carbon intensity `CI` is therefore also
constant at about `0.354` GtCO2 per trillion USD. Fossil emissions `EMIS_F` grow in
lock-step with GDP, from `37.82` Gt in 2023 to about `342` Gt in 2100. That is the
business-as-usual warning: without a rise in the green capital share, decarbonisation
never starts.

cells.title: Baseline variable summary
cells.more:
Use the period selector to read 2023 (period 1) against later years. Deposits `D`
equal loans `L` at every date (the watertightness check). Green capital remains a
small slice of `K` — about `63` against `920` of conventional capital in 2023 —
which is why intensity never falls on this path.

cells.title: Green investment shock
cells.source: This scenario cuts the green loan rate to `int_G = 0.06`, raises the conventional loan rate to `int_C = 0.10`, and lifts autonomous green investment to `beta_0 = 0.33`. The R code applies those shocks from 2027 on a path that starts in 2023; this notebook applies them after the 2100 baseline state, which is the SFCR `runScenario` convention.
cells.more:
In R, scenario 2 keeps 2023 initials and switches parameters at period 5 (2027).
Here a scenario run starts from the baseline's last period, so the experiment is
"from the 2100 BAU state, make green finance cheaper and conventional finance
dearer." The qualitative mechanism is the same: `beta` jumps, `K_G / K_C` starts
rising, and `CI` falls, which is the SIMPLE story of green investment.

cells.title: Scenario 1 green share, intensity and growth
cells.more:
Watch `beta` step up immediately (the rate gap `int_G - int_C` is now negative, so
it adds to `beta_0`). Carbon intensity `CI` then declines as green capital
accumulates faster than conventional capital. Emissions `EMIS_F` combine that
intensity path with output; leverage `lev` moves with the new loan mix.

cells.title: Degrowth shock
cells.source: This scenario sets `c_1 = 0.94` and `alpha_0 = 0.02`. As with scenario 1, R applies the shock from 2027 on the 2023 path; the notebook applies it from the 2100 baseline state.
cells.more:
The degrowth experiment lowers the propensity to consume out of income and the
autonomous investment rate. The consumption cut is small relative to the calibrated
`c_1` of about `0.945`; the investment cut is the main brake. Growth `g_Y` and the
level of `Y` fall relative to continued BAU from the same 2100 starting point, and
emissions fall because output is lower, not because `CI` improves.

cells.title: Scenario 2 output, growth and emissions
cells.more:
Output and investment step down with the lower `alpha_0`. Carbon intensity `CI`
barely moves, because `beta` is unchanged, so any emissions reduction is a scale
effect. Compare that with scenario 1, where the same engine decarbonises through
composition (`K_G / K_C`) rather than through a smaller economy.
